Adam et al. 2023.summary: Pregnant women and new mothers in South Africa got ten short animated story videos on health by phone.
Adam et al. 2023.result: Mothers' knowledge was only slightly higher, with no clear difference from usual care.

Adam et al. 2025.summary: Adults in the United States watched a 3.5-minute animated story online meant to build hope, confidence and resilience.
Adam et al. 2025.result: The video did not measurably change psychological capital compared with a control video.

Adam et al. 2026.summary: Adults in the United States watched a 3.5-minute animated story online about eating less salt.
Adam et al. 2026.result: Knowledge of sodium risks jumped and intention to cut salt rose modestly two weeks later.

Aladé 2018.summary: Young children in the United States watched about 20 episodes of a children's TV show that features diverse characters doing science and math.
Aladé 2018.result: Children's attitudes toward science and math improved modestly compared with a comparison group.

Anderberg et al. 2024.summary: Villages in Pakistan watched a filmed street-theatre play about child marriage and discussed it, with women, men or both attending.
Anderberg et al. 2024.result: Households that saw it showed small shifts in beliefs and reported outcomes, not clearly distinguishable from chance.

Arias 2019.summary: People in Mexico heard a radio drama against violence against women, either privately or publicly with others.
Arias 2019.result: Overall effects were near zero; any benefit came from hearing it publicly.

Aubrey et al. 2014.summary: Teenage girls watched an episode of MTV's 16 and Pregnant online, then reported their views on teen pregnancy and sexual health.
Aubrey et al. 2014.result: The episode had little effect, with attitudes shifting very slightly away from the intended direction.

Banerjee et al. 2015.summary: Villages in India screened a movie about the benefits of iron-fortified salt, alongside discounts on the salt.
Banerjee et al. 2015.result: Households in villages with the screening were more likely to have tried the fortified salt.

Banerjee et al. 2019.summary: Young people in Nigeria watched episodes of MTV Shuga, a TV drama about HIV and sexual health, at a screening, compared with a different show.
Banerjee et al. 2019.result: Viewers gained knowledge and healthier attitudes, and were more likely to get tested for HIV.

Barsoum et al. 2022.summary: A 13-episode Egyptian TV show about starting a business was shown to young adults, who were encouraged to watch it.
Barsoum et al. 2022.result: The show had limited effects overall, but improved views of women entrepreneurs, especially among men.

Basaran et al. 2019.summary: An interactive HIV-prevention video drama about safer sex, shown online in the US to men who have sex with men.
Basaran et al. 2019.result: Viewers' sense of how common risky sex is among other men moved slightly in the safer direction.

Beach et al. 2016.summary: Cancer patients, survivors and family members in the United States watched an 80-minute filmed play of real phone conversations about cancer.
Beach et al. 2016.result: Viewers felt more confident and supported, and reported more talks about cancer a month later than those who watched a nutrition video.

Bekalu et al. 2019.summary: In a US field experiment, people got flu-prevention information as either a personal story or plain facts in a short message.
Bekalu et al. 2019.result: The story version did worse than plain facts: people learned less and were less convinced the prevention steps worked.

Bilali 2022.summary: In 132 villages in Burkina Faso, people met weekly for 12 weeks to listen to a radio drama about resisting violent extremism.
Bilali 2022.result: Listeners were a bit less accepting of violent extremism and somewhat more willing to act against it.

Bilandzic and Sukalla 2019.summary: Participants in a lab watched an 'eco-dystopian' science fiction film about extreme heat, compared with people who saw no film.
Bilandzic and Sukalla 2019.result: The film raised a sense of personal duty to protect the climate and intentions to act, but not belief measures.

Bjorvatn et al. 2020.summary: A Tanzanian TV series about starting a business was shown on national television; secondary students were encouraged to watch it over about three months.
Bjorvatn et al. 2020.result: Students became somewhat more interested in business, but the show also discouraged spending on further schooling.

Brown et al. 2025.summary: US college students watched one sitcom episode with Black and White characters interacting, or a show with only White characters.
Brown et al. 2025.result: Students who saw the diverse sitcom showed less prejudice toward Black people than those who saw the other show.

Brown et al. 2026.summary: A popular Hausa-language TV drama in northern Nigeria added storylines urging viewers to report election corruption over 13 episodes.
Brown et al. 2026.result: Viewers saw reporting as more helpful, but there was no clear change in knowing how to report or in actually reporting.

Carey et al. 2015.summary: Patients at a sexual health clinic in the United States watched a short video on reducing sexual risk, compared with a general health video.
Carey et al. 2015.result: Risky sexual behavior fell for everyone, but the video made no difference compared with the general health video.

Carpena 2024.summary: Villagers in India attended five weekly film screenings with health role models, with some also offered cash rewards for learning.
Carpena 2024.result: People learned more about health and kept that knowledge a year later, with little clear change in daily health habits.

Cassidy et al. 2024.summary: In rural Pakistan, men, women or both watched a filmed street theatre show and talked about delaying girls' marriage.
Cassidy et al. 2024.result: Child marriages fell when men were targeted, alone or with women, in the households reached.

Cherrington et al. 2015.summary: Low-income African-American smokers in US hospitals saw stories of other smokers who quit, alongside regular quit-smoking care.
Cherrington et al. 2015.result: Smokers who saw the stories were somewhat more likely to try quitting and to plan to quit.

Chittamuru 2017.summary: Young African American adults in the United States followed Reality Check, a 13-episode serial drama about HIV prevention.
Chittamuru 2017.result: The drama did not change attitudes or reported behavior measurably compared with the control.

Chong et al. 2026.summary: Poor rural women in the Peruvian highlands watched a five-episode soap opera about saving, in group viewing sessions.
Chong et al. 2026.result: Women's attitudes toward saving improved and their bank savings were higher one and a half and two years later.

Creel et al. 2011.summary: Villagers in Malawi listened in small groups to Radio Diaries, true stories of people living with HIV, with or without group discussion.
Creel et al. 2011.result: Listeners were less afraid of casual contact with people with HIV and showed less stigma on some measures.

Danila et al. 2018.summary: US women who had broken a bone were sent a video, booklet and phone support using stories to encourage osteoporosis medicine.
Danila et al. 2018.result: It made no real difference to whether women started osteoporosis medicine.

Dione et al. 2026.summary: Adolescent girls and young women in rural Senegal watched episodes of the TV drama C'est la vie! in film clubs, on violence against women and reproductive health.
Dione et al. 2026.result: Girls learned more about the topics, but attitudes moved little and behavior did not change.

Donati et al. 2022.summary: Adults in India got short video episodes via Facebook Messenger, either a comedy drama or a documentary series, about gender norms and violence.
Donati et al. 2022.result: Small gains in knowledge and attitudes after a week, which faded after four months.

Engels et al. 2009.summary: Pairs of young Dutch men watched a movie for an hour in a lab bar, with either many or few alcohol scenes and ads, and could drink freely.
Engels et al. 2009.result: Men who saw more alcohol scenes drank more during the session.

Forster et al. 2016.summary: Hispanic kidney disease patients and family in Southern California watched a bilingual telenovela about kidney transplant and healthy habits.
Forster et al. 2016.result: Patients knew more about kidney disease and said they would take more health steps than those who did not watch.

Foss and Blake 2018.summary: US students watched a clip of a prime-time TV show showing a woman breastfeeding in public.
Foss and Blake 2018.result: Students became more accepting of breastfeeding in public and less likely to see it as private.

Gonzalez 2020.summary: A short telenovela-style video about depression, shown to Spanish-speaking Latina adults with limited English in the US, aimed to cut stigma and improve mental health knowledge.
Gonzalez 2020.result: Knowledge about depression rose clearly, but attitudes toward seeking professional help barely changed.

Graczyk 2019.summary: University students who drink caffeinated alcohol mixes viewed a story-based message about drunk driving in a lab, compared with a plain-facts message.
Graczyk 2019.result: Students who saw the story showed slightly more negative attitudes toward drunk driving than those who saw facts.

Green et al. 2020.summary: Villagers in rural Uganda attended community screenings of video dramas discouraging violence against women and encouraging reporting.
Green et al. 2020.result: Attitudes did not change, but people were more willing to report violence and fewer women experienced it.

Green et al. 2023.summary: Villagers in rural Tanzania listened together to a two-hour radio drama about early and forced marriage.
Green et al. 2023.result: Listeners became somewhat more opposed to early and forced marriage than a comparison group.

Green et al. 2024.summary: Young adults in Indonesian cities watched four condensed episodes of a TV drama about climate change, with discussion.
Green et al. 2024.result: Viewers knew more about climate change and were more willing to act than those who saw an unrelated drama.

Gürbüz et al. 2020.summary: Adults in a Turkish community sample watched a 15-minute video about people living with obsessive-compulsive disorder.
Gürbüz et al. 2020.result: People who watched held much less stigmatizing attitudes toward OCD than the control group.

Harb 2018.summary: Heart patients starting cardiac rehabilitation in the US heard a short success story from a patient who stuck with exercise.
Harb 2018.result: Patients felt more confident about exercising and exercised more regularly than those who did not hear the story.

Hoffman et al. 2017.summary: African American patients in the United States watched a story-style video about colorectal cancer screening before seeing their doctor.
Hoffman et al. 2017.result: Patients' knowledge and attitudes improved, with only a small change in intention to get screened, compared with a video on high blood pressure.

Hopfer 2012.summary: College women viewed a story-based message about HPV vaccination told by peers, doctors or both, then were tracked on vaccination.
Hopfer 2012.result: Little overall difference across versions, though the paper reports higher vaccination for the peer-and-expert version.

Hu et al. 2018.summary: Pregnant women in China were shown a persuasive video about the chickenpox vaccine, compared with a booklet or nothing.
Hu et al. 2018.result: More children of women who saw the video were vaccinated than in the comparison group.

Jain 2011.summary: Online participants in the US watched a short story clip showing a minority group positively or negatively, then rated members of that group.
Jain 2011.result: Attitudes toward the minority group shifted only slightly in the intended direction.

Jenner et al. 2023.summary: Black and Hispanic young women aged 18 to 19 in the US watched a 23-minute sexual health video before a clinic visit.
Jenner et al. 2023.result: Viewers knew more about contraception and showed small gains in protective sexual health behavior after three months.

Jones 2008.summary: Young urban women in the northeastern US watched a 43-minute soap opera video on a handheld computer about reducing HIV risk.
Jones 2008.result: Women who watched were somewhat less likely to expect to have unprotected sex.

Jones et al. 2018.summary: Participants in the US were exposed to dystopian fiction such as The Hunger Games, then answered questions about politics.
Jones et al. 2018.result: Exposure produced small shifts in political attitudes after the dystopian fiction.

Kennedy et al. 2018.summary: African American women in church listening groups in the United States heard a story audio recording about bowel cancer screening, compared with an expert interview.
Kennedy et al. 2018.result: Intention to get screened was about the same or slightly higher after the story; attitudes were lower.

Keum and Ogrodniczuk 2022.summary: Men online watched a 3 to 4 minute first-person video where a man tells his story of depression, compared with a brochure or nothing.
Keum and Ogrodniczuk 2022.result: The video weakened the link between traditional masculine beliefs and negative attitudes toward getting psychological help.

Keum et al. 2025.summary: Latino young adults in the United States watched a 3-minute online video of a Black mother telling how racism affected her son.
Keum et al. 2025.result: Compared with a plain informational video, the story left empathy about the same and slightly raised intentions to speak out against racism.

Kim et al. 2014.summary: College students in the United States watched an episode of the TV drama ER with a short message against binge drinking built in.
Kim et al. 2014.result: Students who saw the episode had more negative attitudes toward binge drinking and stronger intentions to avoid it.

Kreuter et al. 2010.summary: Low-income African American women in St. Louis watched a video of breast cancer survivors' stories or an equivalent factual video about mammograms.
Kreuter et al. 2010.result: The survivor-story video gave small gains in attitudes and intention to get a mammogram over the factual video.

Kriss et al. 2017.summary: Pregnant African American women at prenatal clinics watched a short emotional video about whooping cough vaccination, compared with a tablet booklet and no education.
Kriss et al. 2017.result: More women who saw the video got vaccinated than those in the comparison group, though the small trial left this uncertain.

Lapinski and Nwulu 2008.summary: In Abuja, Nigeria, people watched a short film about HIV to see whether it changes how they see the disease and people living with it.
Lapinski and Nwulu 2008.result: Viewers saw HIV as more serious and showed somewhat less stigma, especially men.

Leshner et al. 2018.summary: Women in a lab in the United States watched short breast cancer survivor testimonies, told as stories or as plain information.
Leshner et al. 2018.result: Story versions did not increase intention to act and did slightly worse than non-story versions.

Moran et al. 2016.summary: In the US, women with low or adequate health literacy watched a story film or a plain-facts film about HPV and cervical cancer.
Moran et al. 2016.result: Both films taught people about HPV and cervical cancer, and the story film taught somewhat more.

Mousa et al. 2026.summary: People in Upper Egypt watched a 90-minute state-backed TV drama against female genital cutting and early marriage, or a placebo story.
Mousa et al. 2026.result: The drama increased opposition to genital cutting; effects for early marriage and family planning were weaker.

Moyer-Gusé and Nabi 2011.summary: College students in the United States watched a TV drama episode that modeled safer sex, compared with an education or entertainment-only show.
Moyer-Gusé and Nabi 2011.result: Results were mixed: attitudes and a behavior measure improved, while intentions were lower than in the comparison.

Moyer-Gusé et al. 2019.summary: A funny TV episode with an environmental storyline was shown to participants in the US, then they reported eco-friendly intentions and actions.
Moyer-Gusé et al. 2019.result: Viewers reported more eco-friendly intentions and behavior than people who saw an unrelated show.

Mulligan and Habel 2011.summary: Students in the United States watched the film Cider House Rules, which portrays abortion after incest in a pro-choice light, in a lab.
Mulligan and Habel 2011.result: Viewers' opinions on abortion shifted toward the film's pro-choice view compared with people who did not see it.

Murphy et al. 2013.summary: Mexican American, African American and white women in the US watched an 11-minute story film or a plain-facts film about cervical cancer prevention.
Murphy et al. 2013.result: The story film raised knowledge and attitudes toward Pap tests more, but did not change intentions to get tested.

Murphy et al. 2015.summary: Women in Los Angeles were randomly shown an 11-minute story film or a plain-facts film about preventing and detecting cervical cancer, then followed up.
Murphy et al. 2015.result: The story film gave small gains in attitudes, knowledge and screening behavior compared with the plain-facts film.

Murrar 2018.summary: College students watched a TV comedy episode showing pro-diversity attitudes, then answered questions about people from minority groups in the US.
Murrar 2018.result: Viewers showed somewhat less prejudice and more helping toward minority groups than people who watched a neutral show.

Murrar and Brauer 2018.summary: US students watched a TV sitcom with relatable Arab and Muslim characters, and in a second test a 4-minute music video, to see if prejudice dropped.
Murrar and Brauer 2018.result: Prejudice toward Arabs and Muslims fell more than in the comparison group, with a small shift in willingness to act.

Nera et al. 2018.summary: Participants watched an episode of the TV show The X-Files (about 44 minutes) or a shorter clip online, then answered questions about belief in conspiracy theories.
Nera et al. 2018.result: The conspiracy-themed episode did not make people believe more in real-world conspiracies.

O'Donnell et al. 2010.summary: Parents of sixth-grade girls in New York City got a set of audio CDs at home with stories and tips on talking about sex and alcohol.
O'Donnell et al. 2010.result: Girls reported less sexual risk and drinking, and parents talked with them more on these topics.

Orozco-Olvera and Rascon-Ramirez 2023.summary: Parents in northern Nigeria attended two community screenings of short clips on the value of schooling, followed by discussion.
Orozco-Olvera and Rascon-Ramirez 2023.result: Children were much less likely to be out of school a year later, and attitudes shifted slightly.

Paluck and Green 2009.summary: A year-long radio soap opera in Rwanda showed people speaking up to leaders and resolving disputes; communities listened together.
Paluck and Green 2009.result: Listeners spoke up and disagreed more, and their views on dissent and settling disputes shifted toward the show's message.

Perciful and Meyer 2017.summary: Participants watched one of three films about a person with schizophrenia (accurate, likeable but inaccurate, or fear-based) or a neutral film, in the US.
Perciful and Meyer 2017.result: Less stigma on average across the films, but the fear-based film increased stigma.

Randolph 2019.summary: Adults in the United States watched an online video of farmers telling personal stories about food safety, compared with a fact-based video.
Randolph 2019.result: The story videos did not do better than the fact-based videos; attitudes toward food safety practices were slightly lower.

Reddan et al. 2024.summary: US adults watched the feature film Just Mercy online, about a lawyer defending wrongly convicted people, then took empathy and policy tasks.
Reddan et al. 2024.result: Viewers felt more empathy for formerly incarcerated people and supported criminal justice reform more.

Riley 2024.summary: Secondary students in Uganda watched the film Queen of Katwe, about a girl chess champion, right before national exams.
Riley 2024.result: Students who saw the film did somewhat better on exams, especially in math.

Robison 2013.summary: Participants in the United States watched episodes of TV dramas showing therapy, compared with other shows, to see if it changed views on getting help.
Robison 2013.result: Watching therapy on TV did not raise positive attitudes or intentions to seek therapy.

Sangalang et al. 2019.summary: Online participants in the US read a story that corrected a false health claim about organic tobacco.
Sangalang et al. 2019.result: The story reduced belief in the false claim and weakened intentions based on it more than a plain correction.

SantaMaria et al. 2026.summary: Villagers in rural Tanzania heard a 1.5-minute radio drama about reporting domestic violence in a survey.
SantaMaria et al. 2026.result: The drama made people more willing to tell victims to go to the police; other attitudes did not change.

Scaglioni et al. 2024.summary: Online participants in Italy watched a video of two people telling their colorectal cancer screening stories, or an unrelated video.
Scaglioni et al. 2024.result: The story video did not raise intention to get screened; results were slightly lower, not clearly different.

Semakula et al. 2020.summary: Parents in Uganda listened to a podcast with episodes teaching how to judge claims about treatments, compared with ordinary health announcements.
Semakula et al. 2020.result: A year later, parents were still better at judging whether health claims could be trusted.

Shreedhar et al. 2024.summary: UK adults watched an animated climate story of about five minutes, compared with text, audio or unrelated stories, and could donate to charity.
Shreedhar et al. 2024.result: The animated story led to somewhat more donations to climate charities, with small gains in intentions.

Siddique et al. 2024.summary: Bengali villagers in Bangladesh watched a 45-minute documentary about the Santal minority at community screenings.
Siddique et al. 2024.result: Villagers behaved more kindly toward the minority, but stereotypes and discriminatory views did not change.

Sim et al. 2025.summary: Migrant parents from Myanmar in Thailand watched a 66-minute drama film about parenting, followed by a group discussion.
Sim et al. 2025.result: Small improvements in attitudes and parenting, with less violence against children.

Tisinger 2010.summary: People watched an hour-long TV drama episode touching on public policy, then reported political attitudes in a lab.
Tisinger 2010.result: Viewers' political attitudes shifted in the direction of the episode's message, by a moderate amount.

Toole 2010.summary: Students in a lab watched a clip from a TV drama with pro-environment themes, compared with a clip without them, in the United States.
Toole 2010.result: Attitudes toward the environment improved a little, but beliefs about what others do and approve of moved the other way.

Toole 2014.summary: Participants watched a TV clip in which a character modeled safe sex, to see whether it changed what they thought others consider normal.
Toole 2014.result: It made essentially no difference to how people saw safe-sex norms.

Ungwang et al. 2026.summary: Households in rural Sierra Leone heard an 8-minute peace radio story about farmers and herders during a survey.
Ungwang et al. 2026.result: The short story did not change trust or cooperation between groups.

Vandormael et al. 2021.summary: Adults in the United Kingdom watched a short animated story online about the harm of added sugar, compared with unrelated videos.
Vandormael et al. 2021.result: Viewers reported somewhat stronger intentions to cut back on added sugar.

Vogt et al. 2016.summary: In Sudan, people watched a roughly 90-minute film with a story about female genital cutting, then were tested on their attitudes toward uncut girls.
Vogt et al. 2016.result: Attitudes toward uncut girls moved in the intended direction, by a moderate amount.

Vyas et al. 2025.summary: Mothers-in-law in India watched a short film showing that the father's chromosome decides a baby's sex, not the mother's.
Vyas et al. 2025.result: Women who saw the film learned the fact much more often and blamed daughters-in-law slightly less for having girls.

Watts et al. 2025.summary: Participants in the US watched a Grey's Anatomy clip about medicated abortion or an explainer video with the same facts.
Watts et al. 2025.result: The drama clip did not teach more than the explainer; knowledge was slightly lower, with no clear difference.

Wieland et al. 2024.summary: Hispanic adults in the United States with poorly controlled diabetes watched a 12-minute video of patients telling their own stories.
Wieland et al. 2024.result: Blood sugar control was no better than for the comparison group.

Wilke et al. 2020.summary: Short video dramas (3 to 8 minutes) were shown in rural Ugandan villages on teacher absence, violence against women and abortion stigma; researchers also looked for effects on neighbors.
Wilke et al. 2020.result: Viewers became a little more willing to act on the issues, with little sign the effects spread to others.

Wilke et al. 2022.summary: Ugandans watched three short dramatic videos about teacher absenteeism and whether communities should act on it.
Wilke et al. 2022.result: Viewers were more willing to take action against teacher absenteeism than those who saw other videos.

Yan 2017.summary: Urban Chinese adults read online stories or plain descriptions, positive or negative, about migrant workers, then answered questions about stigma.
Yan 2017.result: Reading a positive story reduced stigma toward migrant workers more than reading a plain description of them.

Yount et al. 2022.summary: Male university students in Vietnam took a six-part web program with a locally made serial drama on consent and bystander action.
Yount et al. 2022.result: Men reported less sexually violent behavior and more bystander action than the comparison group.

Zhang 2008.summary: US adults watched one episode of a TV drama about race relations in a lab, then answered questions about their views of Black Americans.
Zhang 2008.result: Viewers held somewhat more positive attitudes toward Black people and placed more value on equality than the comparison group.

Zhao 2014.summary: Young adults watched excerpts of the teen TV drama 90210 with a storyline about bipolar disorder, compared with a public service ad and a no-storyline version.
Zhao 2014.result: Viewers of the storyline were more willing to engage with the issue, with only a tiny change in behavior.
